When I joined this group I was given an organisation chart with about two hundred names on it, and it was completely useless. Not wrong, just useless. It tells you who reports to whom, and that is almost never the question you have. The question you have is who is the person who actually knows how this gets approved. It took me a year to build the second map, the one that is not written down anywhere, and it looks nothing like the first. There is a woman in the legal division who has been there nineteen years and who can answer in four minutes a question that takes the official channel three weeks. There is an analyst in the region where most of our volume sits who knows every distributor personally. My advice to anybody joining a company this size is to stop reading the chart and start asking one question in every conversation: who is the person to talk to about this? Ask it fifty times and you will have something the chart cannot give you.

People ask me what makes a wine region, and they expect me to say the grape. It is almost never the grape. It is the place, and mostly it is the soil and what happens at night. Take a valley where the days are hot and the nights are cold. That difference is what keeps the acidity in the fruit, and acidity is what makes a wine that you can still drink with food twenty years later. Now take the same grape variety and plant it on a flat, warm plain, and you get something completely different and usually less interesting. This is why a region that nobody has heard of can be more exciting than a famous one. The famous names were mostly decided in the nineteenth century by whoever had a river to move barrels down. The interesting places today are the ones which have the right soil, the right nights and no reputation yet, and which are still run by families who cannot afford to make a wine that tastes like everybody else's.
